title: Peter Was Sinking and Had Time for Only Three Words: “Lord, Save Me!”
paragraphs: Peter Was Sinking and Had Time for Only Three Words: “Lord, Save Me!”
He had enough faith to step out of the boat… but not enough strength to keep himself above the water. What Jesus did next is the Gospel in miniature.
There are prayers you pray when everything is peaceful.
And then there are prayers you pray when you are drowning.
No time to explain what went wrong.
Not in the way we sometimes say, “I feel like I’m drowning.”
He was actually going down into the water.
And perhaps that is why this moment recorded in Matthew 14 is so painfully beautiful.
Because when everything unnecessary was stripped away, Peter discovered what desperate people have been discovering for centuries:
When you cannot save yourself, the name you need is Jesus.

Matthew tells us that after feeding the multitude, Jesus made His disciples get into a boat while He went away to pray. During the night, the boat was battered by the waves because the wind was against them.
Then, through the darkness, Someone came walking toward them.
They thought they were seeing a ghost.
“Take heart; it is I. Do not be afraid.”
Peter answered Him with one of the boldest requests in Scripture:
“Lord, if it is you, command me to come to you on the water.”
Jesus did not give Peter a lecture.
Think about that before remembering how the story ends.
Peter actually climbed out of the boat.
His feet touched something that should not have supported him.
For a moment, the impossible was beneath his feet because his attention was fixed upon Christ.
We often remember Peter as the disciple who sank.
Jesus also remembered him as the disciple who got out of the boat.
Matthew 14:30 tells us that when Peter saw the strength of the wind, he became afraid.
And beginning to sink, he cried out.
The Greek preserves the raw simplicity of his prayer:
There is no performance left in that sentence.
Peter does not tell Jesus why he deserves another chance.
He does not remind Jesus that he was courageous enough to leave the boat.
He does not promise that if Jesus rescues him, he will never doubt again.
Maybe that prayer feels more familiar than you would like to admit.
Maybe nobody knows how close you have been to sinking.
You still know the worship songs.
You still know which Bible verses to quote when somebody else is hurting.
But somewhere beneath the version of yourself everybody sees, you are tired.
You promised God you would stop.
And somewhere along the way, shame whispered something poisonous:
“You cannot call Jesus now. Look at what you have become.”
But Peter's story destroys that lie.
Because Peter did not wait until he had climbed back into the boat before calling Jesus.
He called Jesus while he was sinking.
Some people believe they must repair themselves before returning to Christ.
But drowning people cannot perform surgery on themselves.
And the Gospel begins with a devastating truth to human pride:

Sin is not merely a collection of embarrassing mistakes requiring better habits. Scripture describes humanity apart from Christ as spiritually dead in trespasses and sins. We need more than inspiration.
And His name is Jesus Christ.
Notice what happens after Peter cries out.
“Jesus immediately reached out his hand and took hold of him.”
They did not exhaust Jesus' power.
And there is something here that wounded believers desperately need to understand.
He asked him why he doubted.
Grace does not pretend unbelief is harmless.
Grace does not rename sin so we can remain comfortable in it.
Jesus loves us too much to leave our hearts unchallenged.
Jesus caught Peter before He corrected Peter.
The rebuke came from the One whose hand was already holding him.
Biblical conviction is not Jesus standing safely in the boat shouting instructions to a drowning man.
Christ reached toward the sinking disciple.
And ultimately, what happened on that sea points us toward something infinitely greater.
Because Peter's deepest problem was never water.
Our deepest problem is sin and separation from a holy God.
And Jesus came for drowning sinners.
He did not merely stand at a distance and tell humanity to try harder.
“The Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1:14).
He lived the righteous life we have failed to live.
He went willingly to the cross.
There, the sinless Son of God bore sin.
And on the third day, He rose again.
The Gospel is not that good people managed to swim to God.
The Gospel is that God came to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
That changes the way we read Peter's desperate prayer.
Those words belong beside every hidden failure you thought disqualified you.
Beside the addiction nobody knows about.
Beside the bitterness you have been feeding for years.
Beside the pornography you promised yourself you would never watch again.
The fear that you have wandered too far.
Jesus did not rescue Peter so Peter could remain underwater.
And Jesus does not save sinners so that we can make peace with the very sin from which He came to redeem us.
The Gospel does not say, “Your sin does not matter.”
Sin mattered enough that Christ died.
But the empty tomb announces something even greater:
Your sin does not have to have the final word.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back for mercy.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who alone can give mercy.
Maybe you have spent years trying to make your scandal the final chapter.
This is the same Peter who would later swear that he did not know Jesus.
He had confessed Jesus as the Christ.
And when pressure came, Peter collapsed.
Only this time there was no sea beneath him.
There was simply the horrifying realization that he had denied the Lord he loved.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
If Scripture ended Peter's story there, many of us would understand.
But Jesus was not finished writing.
After the resurrection, Christ restored Peter.
The man who denied Jesus became a public witness to Jesus.
The mouth that once said, in effect, “I do not know Him,” would boldly proclaim the crucified and risen Christ.
It does not pretend the scandal never happened.
It refuses to let the scandal become the final sentence.
From scandal to grace… because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe the person everyone thinks you are and the person you know yourself to be have become painfully different.
The answer is not hiding better.
The answer is not religious acting.
The answer is not another promise to become worthy of Jesus.
Trust the One who died and rose again.
There is no sin made righteous by secrecy, and there is no repentant sinner beyond the sufficiency of Christ's grace.
You may be closer to Peter than you realized.
The failure you thought you had conquered.
And suddenly the faith that once felt strong feels frighteningly small.
Perhaps your prayer tonight does not need to be impressive.
Perhaps it only needs to be honest.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail. But you also do not have to pretend you are invincible.
Someone reading the comments may discover that they are not the only person still fighting to believe.
And somebody on your Facebook friends list may be sinking quietly right now.
They may be smiling in their profile picture.
And privately wondering whether Jesus still wants them.
Not because sharing a post earns favor with God. It does not.
Not because clicking “share” proves your Christianity. It does not.
Send it privately to the person who has gone quiet.
Supporting Gospel-centered work can be one practical expression of generosity and partnership in spreading biblical truth, though our ultimate allegiance and glory belong to Christ alone.
But the deepest reason to stay connected is not merchandise.
A community continually being pointed away from itself and back toward Jesus Christ.
Your hope is not in the strength of your grip on Jesus.
Peter discovered that while disappearing beneath the waves.
He did not have a sermon.
Perhaps that is the picture you need to carry with you tonight.
Not Peter walking spectacularly across the water.
And the hand of Christ reaching toward him.
Because Christianity was never the story of people impressive enough to walk on water.
It is the story of sinners helpless enough to need a Savior…
and a Savior merciful enough to reach them.
So stop pretending you are not sinking.
Then tell somebody else where rescue is found.
The water may remember where Peter sank, but eternity remembers the hand that pulled him out.
